extracted.intended_audience: improvisers, improv students and teachers, theatre performers learning TheatreSports
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for performing Theatresports-style improvisational scenes and games, with emphasis on ensemble skills, audience interaction, and specific game-based constraints. Useful for performers, directors, and teachers running competitive improv shows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word at a Time Story — being 'in the moment'
rubrics_metrics.description: Two or more improvisers alternate words as they tell a story. It teaches the skill of being 'in the moment' (not planning ahead).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not plan ahead because you cannot anticipate others' directions; focus on immediate offers and flow. If done well, the game is entertaining; anti-pattern is trying to preplan lines or control the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yes, Let's — acceptance and positive attitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Each improviser in a scene makes a suggestion that is loudly accepted by the others on stage with the words 'Yes, Let's'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaches acceptance of suggestions by other improvisers and the value of a positive attitude on stage. Anti-pattern: rejecting or negating offers which blocks scene development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guess My Word — alertness and listening
rubrics_metrics.description: An improviser leaves; audience suggests a secret word; the improviser returns and tries to guess the word as suggested by another improviser in the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaches improvisers to be alert to the actions and verbal clues of others; skill is in giving subtle hints and noticing them. Anti-pattern: performers who ignore partners' signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status Switch — awareness and manipulation of status
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvisers create a scene with an obvious high-low status relationship and before the end that relationship must be reversed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaches awareness of character status levels and how to flip them for dramatic effect (example: meek customer turns the tables on the bank owner). Use status shifts to create satisfying arcs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre Replay — stylistic adaptability
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience chooses different styles and the same scene is repeated and altered to reflect each style in turn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests performers' ability to reinterpret the same material in different genre/tonal frameworks; guidance is to clearly mark stylistic changes and commit to style-specific choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puppets / Torture Puppets — working with physical constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Players act as puppets who aren't allowed to move independently (apart from speaking); other players or audience members physically move them. Variation 'Torture Puppets' has one puppeteer manipulate two or more puppets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaches physical control, surrender, and reactive listening; work on clear physical storytelling and cooperating with puppeteers. Anti-pattern: improvisers who try to move independently or ignore the puppeteer's choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alphabet — constraint-based sentence construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Players play out the scene using sentences beginning with successive letters of the alphabet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages linguistic creativity, timing, and keeping the scene coherent under rule constraints. Example dialogue shows how sentences must follow letter order; anti-pattern is breaking the alphabetical sequence or forcing awkward lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper Chase / Papers — integrating audience prompts
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience members write brief sentences on scraps of paper; improvisers begin a scene and at regular intervals read a scrap and work it into the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests ability to incorporate external, possibly incongruous material smoothly (example insert: 'The moon on the lake makes me think of your thighs'). Guidance: blend prompts naturally into scene action rather than stopping the flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction — economy and compression of story
rubrics_metrics.description: Players act out a scene in 45 seconds, then re-perform the same scene in successively shorter times: 30, 20, 10, 5, and finally 3 seconds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaches distillation of essential story beats and comic timing; focus on conveying the core through minimal beats. Anti-pattern: attempting to replicate full dialogue at each shorter length instead of compressing content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional Rollercoaster — emotional flexibility and integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Players act out a scene normally until the M.C. calls out an emotion (e.g., anger or joy); performers must entwine that emotion into their performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests rapid emotional switching and layering of new affects onto established behavior; guidance is to weave the emotion organically rather than overacting to the cue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical Replay — re-contextualization
rubrics_metrics.description: Players act out a scene in 45 seconds, then have to act out the same scene but at a certain date in history (e.g., the French Revolution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests ability to adapt content to a new historical context while maintaining core relationships; use period-appropriate choices to reframe jokes and stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional Replay — reacting with a specified emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar to Historical Replay: players act out a scene in 45 seconds then re-act it using a specified emotion they need to use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes the impact of emotional lens on the same material; guidance is to find new beats and meanings through the chosen emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacejump — rapid re-contextualization and ensemble takeovers
rubrics_metrics.description: One person starts in the center performing an action inside a ring; anyone can call 'spacejump' to freeze them and then take over, restarting the piece in a different direction while adapting to the frozen pose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in large groups to train quick reinterpretation, physical listening, and smooth handoffs. Play continues with multiple people entering and exiting; guidance: adapt to the pose and maintain continuity. Anti-pattern: ignoring the pose or failing to adapt directionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typing Scene / Typewriter — narrated mime with enacted scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: A typist narrates as they mime typing a story while improvisers jump in to enact scenes and add developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests coordination between narrator and actors; can be used for comedic staging (example 'typist hostage' as a heat moment). Guidance: maintain narrative coherence with enacted scenes and allow the typist's pacing to inform action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endowment Game — collective clue-giving and deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: A player attempts to guess facts or information the other improvisers and audience already 'know'; other improvisers give hints through dialogue and the audience signals proximity with 'ooing' and applause when correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaches subtle hinting, collaborative scaffolding, and audience-inclusive storytelling. Variations include Crime Endowment, Gibberish Endowment, Superhero Endowment. Guidance: give progressively clearer clues and use audience reactions as cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish a 'platform' early and respect the 'circle of possibilities'
rubrics_metrics.description: Technique taught by Johnstone: establish a platform early that defines characters and background, then introduce a wrinkle; a scene involves an ever-shrinking 'circle of possibilities' and improvisers should not step outside it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start by defining who, where, and what; as offers accumulate, narrow plausible future offers. Anti-pattern: making offers inconsistent with previously established facts or breaking the reality of the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build characters and collaborative storytelling; avoid corniness/gags
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy: Theatresports emphasizes building characters and spontaneous, collaborative storytelling. Corniness and gags tend to lower scene quality; jokes and gags are seen as disrupting the narrative and avoiding collaboration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize character choices and truthful responses over one-off gags. Anti-pattern: prioritizing cheap jokes or gimmicks that derail scene commitment and ensemble work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generate 'heat' through skilled, staged rule-breaking and audience engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical examples of heat include encouraging the audience to boo the judges, an improviser protesting a low score and being ejected, or performers being 'punished' (e.g., forced to act as a pig).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skillful rule-breaking and audience participation can increase dramatic effect and entertainment value; use provocation and risk to create energy but manage consequences and ensemble safety. Examples: typist hostage, homemade protest signs, judges as stern authority figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of improvised themes and varied constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Shows commonly use challenges such as: scenes involving an object given by an audience member; all dialogue in gibberish; starting and ending with audience-suggested phrases; summarising a major movie in one minute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests performers' ability to meet format constraints while maintaining narrative coherence; guidance is to incorporate constraints as creative fuel rather than allowing them to derail character and relationship work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitive format: scoring by audience or trained judges
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposing teams perform scenes based on audience suggestions, with ratings by the audience or by a panel of judges (who are usually trained improvisers themselves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format note: performances may be judged and scored; judges often play the role of stern authority figures to create dramatic tension and structure. Consider how scoring influences risk-taking and theatrical choices.
